tip: 'Fare la spesa' is the set phrase for grocery shopping: 'faccio la spesa'. The plural 'fare le spese' means clothes shopping.
Adjectives ending in '-e' use '-i' for the plural in both genders: 'felici' = happy, from 'felice'.
'Potrei' is the polite could I: 'potrei avere il menu?' = could I have the menu, softer than 'posso'.
'Potremmo', the conditional of 'potere', makes a request polite: 'potremmo avere il conto?' = could we have the bill? gentler than 'possiamo'.
'Frutta' is a feminine collective noun and stays singular even for many pieces: 'più frutta' = more fruit, not 'frutte'.
Add '-mente' to an adjective to make an adverb, like English -ly: 'lento' becomes 'lentamente' = slowly.
'Sapere' plus an infinitive means to know how to: 'sa cucinare' = he can cook. 'potere' would mean is allowed to.
'Vorremmo' is the polite 'we would like', softer than 'vogliamo' (we want): 'vorremmo ordinare' = we would like to order.
The conditional can flag unconfirmed news: 'pioverebbe' = 'supposedly it will rain', marking it as merely reported, not certain.
Telling time is plural: 'che ore sono?' = what time is it, answered 'sono le tre'. Only one o'clock is singular: 'è l'una'.
'Molto' as adverb is invariable: 'lavoro molto' (I work a lot). As adjective it agrees: 'molte persone' (many people).
Verbs ending in '-giare' drop the 'i' in the future and conditional: 'mangiare' becomes 'mangerei', never 'mangierei'.
'Sarebbe meglio' plus an infinitive softens advice: 'sarebbe meglio partire' = 'it would be better to leave', gentler than a flat command.
'Lungo' means 'long' as an adjective but 'along' before a noun: 'cammino lungo il fiume' = I walk along the river.
'Vicino' needs 'a' after it: 'abitiamo vicino al parco'. English 'near the park' has no preposition, but Italian adds the 'a'.
Italian makes routine verbs reflexive: 'si prepara' = she prepares herself (gets ready), where English just says 'gets ready'.
'In' contracts with articles: 'in' + 'il' = 'nel', 'in' + 'la' = 'nella'. 'nel giardino' = in the garden. Mandatory with definite articles.
An article on a time word signals a habit: 'la sera guardo un film' = in the evenings, every evening, I watch a movie.
'Ogni' never changes form, and before a number it takes a plural noun: 'ogni cinque minuti' = every five minutes.
'Sapere' has an irregular subjunctive, 'sappia', used after 'dubito che': 'dubito che lui sappia'.
'Fare attenzione', literally 'to make attention', means to pay attention: 'faccia attenzione'.
Spending time is 'passare'; 'spendere' is only for money. 'passiamo le vacanze' = we spend the holidays.
'Stare' covers how you are doing: 'sta peggio di ieri' = she is feeling worse than yesterday. Health and mood take 'stare'.
Italian uses 'stare', not 'essere', for body position: 'stiamo seduti' = we are sitting.
'Ci vediamo' is literally we see each other, the normal way to say see you later.
The object pronoun can sit before the modal or attach to the infinitive: 'mi puoi aiutare' = 'puoi aiutarmi', both fine.
'Servire' works like 'piacere': in 'ti serve aiuto', 'aiuto' is the subject and 'ti' is who needs it.
'Cos'hai' is 'cosa' + 'hai': 'cosa' drops its final '-a' before the vowel of 'hai'. 'cos'hai fatto' = what did you do.
'Uscire' takes 'da' for leaving a place: 'esce dal lavoro' = he leaves work.
Lateness is a fixed phrase with 'essere': 'essere in ritardo' = to be late, so 'siamo in ritardo'.
